{{Short description|Problem in mathematical optimisation}}
In [[mathematical optimization]], '''Zermelo's navigation problem''', proposed in 1931 by [[Ernst Zermelo]], is a classic [[optimal control]] problem that deals with a boat navigating on a body of water, originating from a point <math>A</math> to a destination point <math>B</math>. The boat is capable of a certain maximum speed, and the goal is to derive the best possible control to reach <math>B</math> in the least possible time.
[[File:Zermelo Navigation under constant wind.png|thumb|Zermelo Navigation with velocity <math>\mathbf v</math>under constant wind <math>\mathbf{w}</math>]]
Without considering external forces such as current and wind, the optimal control is for the boat to always head towards <math>B</math>. Its path then is a [[line segment]] from <math>A</math> to  <math>B</math>, which is trivially optimal. With consideration of current and wind, if the combined force applied to the boat is non-zero the control for no current and wind does not yield the optimal path.

==History==
In his 1931 article,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Zermelo|first1=Ernst|title=Über das Navigationsproblem bei ruhender oder veränderlicher Windverteilung|journal=Zeitschrift für Angewandte Mathematik und Mechanik|date=1931|volume=11|issue=2|pages=114–124|bibcode=1931ZaMM...11..114Z|doi=10.1002/zamm.19310110205}}</ref> Ernst Zermelo formulates the following problem:
{{Quote| text=In an unbounded plane where the wind distribution is given by a vector field as a function of position and time, a ship moves with constant velocity relative to  the surrounding air mass. How must the ship be steered in order to come from a  starting point to a given goal in the shortest time?}}
[[File:Ernst Zermelo 1900s.jpg|thumb|Ernst Zermelo formulated and solved the general problem]]

This is an extension of the classical optimisation problem for [[geodesics]] –
minimising the length of a curve <math> I[c] = \int_a^b \sqrt{1 +y'^2}\, d x</math> 
connecting points <math> A</math>  and <math> B</math> , with the added complexity of considering some wind velocity. Although it is usually impossible to find an exact solution in most cases, the general case was solved by Zermelo himself in the form of a [[partial differential equation]], known as Zermelo's equation, which can be numerically solved.

The problem of navigating an airship which is surrounded by air, was presented first in 1929 at a conference by Ernst Zermelo, who was inspired by the circumnavigation of [[LZ 127 Graf Zeppelin|Graf Zeppelin]] in 1929-08. Other mathematicians have answered the challenge over the following years. The dominant technique for solving the equations is the [[calculus of variations]].<ref name="Ebbinghaus2007">{{cite book|author=Heinz-Dieter Ebbinghaus|title=Ernst Zermelo: An Approach to His Life and Work|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pDkLizKAQZQC&pg=PA152|date=2 June 2007|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-3-540-49553-6|pages=150–}}</ref>

==Constant-wind case==

The case of constant wind is easy to solve exactly.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Warnick|first1=Claude|title=The geometry of sound rays in a wind|journal=Contemporary Physics|date=2011|volume=52|issue=3|pages=197–209|doi=10.1080/00107514.2011.563515|arxiv=1102.2409|bibcode=2011ConPh..52..197G|s2cid=119728138}}</ref>
Let <math>\mathbf d = \vec{AB}</math>, and suppose that to minimise the travel time the ship 
travels at a constant maximum speed <math>V</math>. Thus the position of the ship at 
time <math>t</math> is <math>\mathbf x = t(\mathbf v + \mathbf w)</math>. Let <math>T</math> be the time of arrival at <math>B</math>, so that <math>\mathbf d = T(\mathbf v + \mathbf w)</math>. Taking the [[dot product]] of this with <math>\mathbf w</math> and <math>\mathbf d</math> respectively results in 
<math> \vec d \cdot \vec w = T(\mathbf v \cdot \vec w + \mathbf w^2)
</math> and <math> d^2 = T^2(v^2 + 2\vec v \cdot \mathbf w + \mathbf w^2)	
</math>. Eliminating <math>\vec v \cdot \vec w</math> and writing this system as a quadratic in <math>T</math> results in <math>(\vec v^2 - \vec w^2)T^2 + 2(\mathbf d\cdot \mathbf w)T - \mathbf d^2 = 0</math>. Upon solving this, taking the positive square-root since <math>T</math> is positive, we obtain

: <math>
\begin{align}
T[\mathbf d] & = \frac{-2(\mathbf d \cdot \mathbf w) \pm \sqrt{4(\mathbf d \cdot \mathbf w)^2 + 4\mathbf d^2(\mathbf v^2 - \mathbf w^2)}}{2(\mathbf v^2 - \mathbf w^2)} \\[8pt]
& = \sqrt{\frac{\mathbf d^2}{\mathbf v^2 - \vec w^2} + \frac{(\mathbf d \cdot \mathbf w)^2}{(\vec v^2 - \vec w^2)^2}} - \frac{\mathbf d \cdot \mathbf w}{\mathbf v^2 - \mathbf w^2}
\end{align}
</math>

Claim: This defines a metric on <math>\mathbb R^2</math>, provided <math>|\mathbf v| > |\mathbf w|</math>.

===Proof===

By our assumption, clearly <math>T[\mathbf d] \geq 0</math> with equality if and only if <math>\mathbf d =0</math>. Trivially if <math>\tilde{\mathbf d}  = \vec{BA}</math>, we have <math>T[\mathbf d] = T[\tilde{\mathbf d}]</math>. It remains to show <math>T</math> satisfies a [[triangle inequality]] <math>T[\mathbf d_1 + \mathbf d_2] \leq T[\mathbf d_1] + T[\mathbf d_2]. </math>

Indeed, letting <math>c^2 := \mathbf v^2 - \mathbf w^2</math>, we note that this is true if and only if

: <math>
\begin{align}
& \sqrt{\frac{(\mathbf d_1+\mathbf d_2)^2}{c^2} + \frac{((\vec d_1+\vec d_2) \cdot \vec w)^2}{c^4}} - \frac{(\mathbf d_1 + \mathbf d_2) \cdot \mathbf w}{c^2} \\[8pt]
\leq {} & \sqrt{\frac{\mathbf d_1^2}{c^2} + \frac{(\mathbf d_1 \cdot \mathbf w)^2}{c^4} - \frac{\mathbf d_2 \cdot \mathbf w}{c^2}} + \sqrt{\frac{\mathbf d_2^2}{c^2} + \frac{(\mathbf d_2 \cdot \mathbf w)^2}{c^4}} - \frac{\mathbf d_2 \cdot \mathbf w}{c^2}
\end{align}
</math>

if and only if

: <math> \frac{\mathbf d_1\cdot \mathbf d_2}{c^2} + \frac{(\mathbf d_1\cdot \mathbf w)( \mathbf d_2 \cdot \mathbf w)}{c^4} \leq \left[\frac{\vec d_1^2}{c^2} + \frac{(\mathbf d_1 \cdot \mathbf w)^2}{c^4} \right]^{1/2} \left[\frac{\vec d_2^2}{c^2} + \frac{(\mathbf d_2 \cdot \mathbf w)^2}{c^4}\right]^{1/2},
</math>

which is true if and only if

: <math> \frac{(\mathbf d_1\cdot \mathbf d_2)^2}{c^4} + \frac{2(\mathbf d_1 \cdot \mathbf d_2)(\mathbf d_1\cdot \mathbf w)(\mathbf d_2 \cdot \mathbf w)}{c^6} \leq \frac{\mathbf d_1^2 \cdot \mathbf d_2^2}{c^4} + \frac{\mathbf d_1^2(\mathbf d_2\cdot \mathbf w)^2+\mathbf d_2^2(\mathbf d_1\cdot \mathbf w)^2}{c^6}
</math>

Using the [[Cauchy–Schwarz inequality]], we obtain <math>(\mathbf d_1 \cdot \mathbf d_2)^2 \leq \mathbf d_1^2 \cdot \mathbf d_2^2 </math> with equality if and only if <math>\mathbf d_1</math> and <math>\mathbf d_2</math> are linearly dependent, and so the inequality is indeed true. <math>\blacksquare</math>

Note: Since this is a strict inequality if <math>\mathbf d_1</math> and 
<math>\mathbf d_2</math> are not linearly dependent, it immediately follows that a straight 
line from <math>A</math> to <math>B</math> is always a faster path than any other path made up of straight line segments. We use a limiting argument to prove this is true for 
any curve.

==General solution==
Consider the general example of a ship moving against a variable wind <math>\vec w(x,y)</math>. Writing this component-wise, we have the drift in the <math>x</math>-axis as <math>u(x,y)</math> and the drift in the <math>y</math>-axis as <math>v(x,y)</math>. Then for a ship moving at maximum velocity <math>V</math> at variable heading <math>\theta</math>, we have

: <math>
\begin{align}
\dot x &= V\cos \theta + u(x,y) \\
\dot y &= V\sin\theta + v(x,y)
\end{align}
</math>

The Hamiltonian of the system is thus

: <math>
H = \lambda_x(V\cos\theta + u) + \lambda_y(V\sin\theta + v) + 1
</math>

Using the [[Euler–Lagrange equation]], we obtain

: <math>
\begin{align}
\dot \lambda_x &= -\frac{\partial H}{\partial x} = -\lambda_x \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} - 
\lambda_y \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\\
\dot \lambda_y &= -\frac{\partial H}{\partial y} = -\lambda_x \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}
- \lambda_y \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \\
0 &= \frac{\partial H}{\partial \theta} = V(-\lambda_x \sin\theta + \lambda_y\cos\theta) 
\end{align}
</math>

The last equation implies that <math>\tan\theta = \lambda_y / \lambda_x</math>. We note that the system is autonomous; the Hamiltonian does not depend on time <math>t</math>, thus <math>H</math> = constant, but since we are minimising time, the constant is equal to 0.  Thus we can solve the simultaneous equations above to get<ref>{{cite book|last1=Bryson|first1=A.E.|title=Applied Optimal Control: Optimization, Estimation and Control|date=1975|publisher=Taylor & Francis|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=P4TKxn7qW5kC|isbn=9780891162285}}</ref>

: <math>
\begin{align}
\lambda_x &= \frac{-\cos\theta}{V + u\cos\theta + v\sin\theta}\\[6pt]
\lambda_y &= \frac{-\sin\theta}{V + u\cos\theta +v\sin\theta}
\end{align}
</math>

Substituting these values into our EL-equations results in the differential 
equation

: <math>
\frac{d \theta}{d t} 
= \sin^2\theta \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} 
+ \sin\theta \cos\theta \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}
\right) - \cos^2\theta\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}	
</math>

This result is known as Zermelo's equation. Solving this with our system allows us to find the general optimum path.

===Constant-wind revisited example===
If we go back to the constant wind problem <math>\mathbf w</math> for all time, we have

: <math>
\frac{\partial v}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = 0
</math>

so our general solution implies  <math>
\frac{d \theta}{d t} = 0 </math>, thus <math> \theta </math> is constant,
i.e. the optimum path is a straight line, as we had obtained before with an 
algebraic argument.
